# Expression type tables

<!-- Generated by tools/exprtables (exprtables page) from the type rule of the
     typing pass (rule P+; programs/blitz2/src/exprtyping.c, the matrix model's
     EM_RULES_DECIDED) and the type decisions of programs/blitz2/src/exprtype.c;
     do not edit.  After a change of the rules, build the target
     expression_type_tables_update and commit this file. -->

These tables list the type rules of an expression in `blitz2` as the compiler
applies them: for one operation of two values, the type each operand is taken
in and the type that results, for every operator, operand type and wanted type.
The rules and the reasons for them are explained in
[The type of an expression in blitz2](expression-types.md); this page only
lists them. It is generated by `tools/exprtables` from the rule of the
compiler's typing pass (`programs/blitz2/src/exprtyping.c`, rule P+ of #1216,
as the expression matrix's model computes it; the host test `blitz2_exprtyping`
checks that the two agree) and, for what that pass does not decide, from the
type decisions of `programs/blitz2/src/exprtype.c`; the build checks that it is
up to date.

## How to read the tables

Every operation is typed by its operator, the types of its two operands and the
*wanted type* ([The operand typing](expression-types.md#the-operand-typing-rule-p-1216)):
the type of the destination of an assignment or of a parameter, Long for an
array index, none for `If`, `While`, `Until`, `Print`, `Select` and the operands
of a comparison. The wanted type reaches every operation of the expression from
the top, so the same operation has the same type in every place of an
expression and the order of the operands does not matter.

Each table is for one operator, or for several that behave the same. A row is
an operation `a OP b` of two values of the types *left* and *right* (a variable,
a function value, or an operation whose result has that type); a column is the
wanted type. A cell `L R → T` says: the left operand is taken as type L, the
right one as type R, and the result has type T. The letters are B Byte, W Word,
L Long, Q Quick, F Float, – none.

* An operand taken as a higher type than its own is converted up first; `↓`
  marks a Quick or Float operand converted down to a whole number (a Quick
  rounded down, a Float truncated towards zero).
* `Q~ Q~ → 48`: a 48.16 operation. Both operands are taken as 48.16 values (a
  whole number with 16 bits of fraction, a register pair), so a Quick and a Long
  or a Quick under a wanted Long are computed exactly; the result is rounded once,
  where the expression's value is taken (a wanted whole number rounded down, a
  `/` at the top towards zero, #1222; a wanted Quick its 16.16 value, no wanted
  type a Quick where it fits, else rounded down to a whole number); a product or
  quotient is cut to 1/65536 in the direction of that rounding (down under a
  wanted whole number, #1221).
* `Q Q → Q` with a Byte or Word operand: a 16.16 operation.
* `illegal`: the compiler refuses the operation ("Illegal Operator for Type").
* † marks a cell that differs when the operands are swapped (listed below
  each table).

The value of the whole expression is converted to the wanted type at the end;
that conversion is not part of the tables. A constant is typed by its own rule
("Constants", below), so an operation with a constant operand follows the row
of the type the constant takes. String operands (`+` and the comparisons take
them) are not shown.

A Quick operand of these operators is taken by its whole part (rounded down, its
fraction bits cleared; #1209), and so is a constant with a point (`1.5 AND 3` is
1) and a 48.16 operand (its whole part as a Long). A Float has none of them.

## Shifts

The right operand is the count. A shift of a Quick works on its 16.16 value, so
the fraction takes part (`x LSR 1` with `x=5` is 2.5).

numbers (a negative remainder has the divisor added): `x.q=b Mod 1.5` with `b=4`
is 1, `f Mod g` with 7.5 and 2 is 1.5. Two whole operands keep the whole-number
`Mod`.

## Comparisons

A comparison gives a Word, its boolean (-1 or 0), also where it compares in
Float. Both operands are typed by their own operands, never by the wanted type
(#1177, #1183), and the lower of the two is converted up to the other; a Long and
a Quick (`L Q`, `Q L`), and a Byte or Word with a Quick, are compared exactly: the
whole number against the whole part of the Quick, on equality the fraction
decides.

## Elements

A variable or a function value keeps its own type until the operation it is an
operand of converts it (the cells above); a Byte value is always extended to a
Word in its register, which is no change of type.

## Constants

A constant takes the type it is wanted in, or the size it needs; it is written in
that type, without conversion code. The cell is the type of a constant alone (an
expression that is only the constant) under the wanted type; "(whole)": a
constant written with a point that is taken as the whole number it is. As an
operand of an operation a constant with a point is fractional, never a whole
number: a Float under a wanted Byte, Word or Long (#1222), else a Quick where a
Quick is in its expression or wanted, else a Float ("Constants beside an
operand", below). A negative constant is the constant with a minus before it.

| constant | kind | – | B | W | L | Q | F |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `5` | a whole number of Byte size | B | B | W | L | Q | F |
| `300` | a whole number of Word size | W | W | W | L | Q | F |
| `100000` | a whole number of Long size | L | L | L | L | L | F |
| `1.5` | a fraction that fits a Quick | F | F | F | F | Q | F |
| `40000.5` | a fraction beyond the Quick range | F | F | F | F | F | F |
| `2.0` | a whole value written with a point | F | B (whole) | F | F | Q | F |
| `300.0` | the same of Word size | F | W (whole) | F | F | Q | F |
| `1e10` | a whole part beyond a Long | F | F | F | F | F | F |

## Constants beside an operand

A constant beside an operand of the type *other* (the columns), with no wanted
type: the type it takes.

| constant | kind | B | W | L | Q | F |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `5` | a whole number of Byte size | B | W | L | Q | F |
| `300` | a whole number of Word size | W | W | L | Q | F |
| `100000` | a whole number of Long size | L | L | L | Q | F |
| `1.5` | a fraction that fits a Quick | F | F | F | Q | F |
| `40000.5` | a fraction beyond the Quick range | F | F | F | F | F |
| `2.0` | a whole value written with a point | F | F | F | Q | F |

## The exceptions and their issues

The rules of the original compiler with the port's fixes of these original
bugs; each is described on [The type of an expression in
blitz2](expression-types.md):

* #978: an equality comparison of a byte value with a constant from 128 to 255
  takes the constant as the byte it stands for ([deviations](deviations.md)).
* #1177, #1183: the operands of a comparison are compared with their own values
  ([A comparison starts again](expression-types.md#a-comparison-starts-again)).
* #1179: an array index after the first is a Long, as the first
  ([Where this is a problem](expression-types.md#where-this-is-a-problem)).
* #1182: a comparison as the right operand is converted up to the left
  operand's type ([A comparison starts again](expression-types.md#a-comparison-starts-again)).
* #1209: `&`, `|`, `AND`, `OR`, `EOR` take a Quick as a whole number ([Bit
  operators under a Quick type so
  far](expression-types.md#bit-operators-under-a-quick-type-so-far-1209)).
* #1216: every operand is typed by its own operands and the wanted type, not by
  its place in the expression ([The operand
  typing](expression-types.md#the-operand-typing-rule-p-1216)).
